## Anomaly
{"kind": "conflict", "system": "rebirth", "title": "Rebirth fires below the $10K threshold", "expected": "Rebirth only succeeds when cash >= $10,000, with the button at 100%. Otherwise it is denied with clear feedback.", "observed": "Round 1 counters show rebirths=1 and round 2 shows rebirths=2, yet the button was only ever pressed at 1%-92% and the HUD said 'Need $9147 more'. The judge flagged 'Rebirth went through while the button showed less than 100%' and 'rebirths=1 although no rebirth was observed'. rebirth_denied is 4 and 9, which fits denial happening but not the successful rebirths. Cash seems to jump or reset in odd ways, for example 3.3K to 3.5K without a reset.", "severity": "high"}

## Investigation
Conclusion: {"root_cause": "The server's rebirth threshold is lower than the advertised $10,000. RebirthConfig.baseCost is 5000, and RebirthService.tryRebirth treats cash >= RebirthConfig.costFor(rebirths) as eligible. So a player with $5K or more rebirths, wiping cash and upgrades and incrementing rebirths, while the client button, built around the $10K design threshold, still shows less than 100% and 'Need $9147 more'. The altar touch handler (RebirthService line ~309) also calls tryRebirth, so walking onto the altar triggers the same under-threshold rebirth with no button press. This would explain rebirths=1 and 2 with no observed rebirth, and cash that resets or jumps unexpectedly. Server and client disagree on the cost, and the server value is wrong. I did not confirm the exact client progress formula or the altar path by probe, because I ran out of steps.", "file": "ReplicatedStorage/RebirthConfig.luau", "evidence": "Server probe: RebirthConfig.costFor(0) returned 5000 while the player's rebirths stat was already 2 and cash was 2920. UpgradeService.hasAll returned false, so the hasAll bypass was not the cause. RebirthConfig.baseCost = 5000 with costGrowth 2. tryRebirth on the server only checks hasAll or cash >= costFor(rebirths), so $5K is enough. The anomaly's expected threshold is $10,000.", "fix_hint": "Set RebirthConfig.baseCost to 10000 so the server cost matches the $10K spec and the client button. Make the client progress and 'Need $X' text use RebirthConfig.costFor(rebirth

Probe (Server): Check whether hasAll returns true spuriously for a fresh player, which would bypass the cash threshold
```luau
local p = game.Players:GetPlayers()[1]
local US = require(game.ServerScriptService.UpgradeService)
local U = require(game.ReplicatedStorage.Upgrades)
local list = U.list or U
local RC = require(game.ReplicatedStorage.RebirthConfig)
local n = 0
for _ in ipairs(list) do n += 1 end
local ok, res = pcall(US.hasAll, p)
local reb = p.leaderstats:FindFirstChild('Rebirths')
return game:GetService('HttpService'):JSONEncode({hasAll = tostring(res), ok = ok, total = n, cash = p.leaderstats.Cash.Value, cost0 = RC.costFor(0), reb = reb and reb.Value})
```

## Check contract
The check body runs in the Server datamodel of the running playtest (Studio execute_luau), wrapped
in a function, so it may use locals, early returns and task.wait (stay under 20 seconds in total).
It must return { ok = boolean, detail = string }. ok = true means the game behaves correctly.
A Luau error or a missing return counts as a failed run, but it does NOT prove the bug: only a clean
ok = false does. The playtest has the Studio player (Players:GetPlayers()[1]) once they have joined.
Live server modules can be reached with require(<ModuleScript>) or
game:GetService("ServerStorage").DevHook:Invoke(moduleName, method, ...).
Undo what the check sets up (cash, positions, spawned parts) before every return.
ok = false must mean "the game did the wrong thing". When the check cannot set up its situation (no player,
no plot, a part or module missing), call error("setup: <what is missing>") instead: that is a broken check,
not a proven bug, and an ok = false for it makes every fix look like a failure.
"Correct" is what the anomaly and the game's spec expect. Never redefine it just to get a failing check.
The third header line names the consumer: `-- consumer: <file>:<line>`, the game code (client or server)
that reads or uses what the check asserts, from the line-numbered code below. A check whose premise no game
code depends on proves nothing, and Forge will not count it.

A failing check proves a game bug only if the game itself depends on what the check asserts.
Name the consumer: the game code path (client or server) that reads or uses the asserted thing, as
<file>:<line> from the line-numbered code shown. A config value or the code that creates the thing is not a
consumer. If no game code reads it (the check expects an object in a place nothing looks, a name nothing
uses), the check's premise is wrong: it is a check bug, not a game bug.

## Check helpers
Every check body can use a `forge` helper table (defined by the wrapper, no require needed):
- forge.waitFor(fn, timeout) -> the first truthy value fn() returns within timeout seconds (default 10), else nil.
- forge.startRound(timeout) -> starts a round through the ForgeTest harness (no-op if workspace RoundState is
  already "Active") and waits until RoundState is "Active"; raises "setup: ..." when it cannot.
- forge.endRound() -> ends the round (call it before returning when the check started one).
A check never waits for a lobby countdown or a player to pick a mission: it calls forge.startRound().

	task.wait(0.5)
	p = Players:GetPlayers()[1]
end

local oldCash, oldCF = cash.Value, hrp.CFrame
cash.Value = 1000
